title: Undo a multiplication on a clock
hook: Times 7 scrambles a 26-hour clock. Which number unscrambles it, and how do you find it?

knows: Euclid's remainders find a greatest common divisor (euclid-leftover-rectangle)
clock arithmetic: numbers wrap around at the clock size
doesNotKnow: that Euclid's steps run backwards write 1 as a mix of 26 and 7
that this mix gives the x with 7x = 1 on a 26-hour clock

misconception: You can undo a multiplication on a clock the way you undo it on a number line, by dividing, or not at all.
objective: The learner can explain that running Euclid on 26 and 7 backwards gives 1 = 3 x 26 - 11 x 7, so -11, which is 15 on the clock, undoes multiplying by 7 (7 x 15 = 105 = 4 x 26 + 1), and that such an undo exists exactly when the gcd is 1.

claims.text: On a 26-hour clock, multiplying by 7 scrambles the hours (each hour goes to a different hour), and x = 15 is the only hour from 0 to 25 with 7x landing on 1: 7 x 15 = 105 = 4 x 26 + 1.
claims.source: Builder's node script (2026-10-14): 7x mod 26 for x = 0..25 hits every residue once (gcd(7, 26) = 1), and only x = 15 gives 1; 105 = 4 x 26 + 1. Demo.tsx computes X = 15 from the back-substitution, not from a search. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: node undo.mjs: 7x mod 26 over x=0..25 hits all 26 residues, only x=15 gives 1; 105 = 4 x 26 + 1. Matches predict key (option 15) and reveal.

claims.text: Euclid on 26 and 7: 26 = 3 x 7 + 5, 7 = 1 x 5 + 2, 5 = 2 x 2 + 1, 2 = 2 x 1 + 0, so the last non-zero remainder (the gcd) is 1. Each row is bigger = q x smaller + remainder.
claims.source: Demo.tsx euclid(26, 7): remainders 26, 7, 5, 2, 1, 0 and quotients 3, 1, 2, 2; builder's node script agrees. Euclid's algorithm: CLRS 4e chapter 31 (section 31.2). · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: node, Demo euclid(26,7) copied: remainders 26 7 5 2 1 0, quotients 3 1 2 2; stage rows j=1..4 print exactly these four equations.

claims.text: Backing up: 1 = 5 - 2 x 2; swapping in 2 = 7 - 1 x 5 gives 1 = -2 x 7 + 3 x 5; swapping in 5 = 26 - 3 x 7 gives 1 = 3 x 26 - 11 x 7.
claims.source: Demo.tsx BACK (back-substitution over the Euclid rows); builder ran the same code in node (2026-10-14): coefficients (1, -2), (-2, 3), (3, -11). Check: 3 x 26 - 11 x 7 = 78 - 77 = 1. Agrees with extended Euclid on (26, 7) giving gcd 1 = 3 x 26 + (-11) x 7. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: node, Demo BACK loop copied: coefficients (1,-2), (-2,3), (3,-11); 78 - 77 = 1. Row text 'swap in 2 = 7 - 1 x 5', 'swap in 5 = 26 - 3 x 7' matches.

claims.text: The 3 x 26 part is whole turns of the clock, so -11 x 7 is 1, and -11 + 26 = 15: 7 x 15 = 105, 4 turns and 1 hour.
claims.source: Reduce 1 = 3 x 26 - 11 x 7 mod 26: 3 x 26 is 0 mod 26, so -11 x 7 = 1 (mod 26); -11 and -11 + 26 = 15 are the same hour. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: Derivation: 3 x 26 = 0 mod 26, so -11 x 7 = 1 mod 26; ((-11 % 26) + 26) % 26 = 15 = Demo X. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v2, wave E r6 revision by demo-builder): stage now has a 26-hour ring and a ×13 chip; reveal reworded and shortened. | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. v2 Demo: back-substitution gives (3, -11); 3 x 26 - 11 x 7 = 1; ((-11 % 26) + 26) % 26 = 15; 7 x 15 = 105 = 4 x 26 + 1. Reveal prints COEF_A = -11, X = 15, floor(105/26) = 4. All 4 milestones (incl. bezout, read-15) are required before the reveal.

claims.text: 11 is the coefficient without its minus sign: 7 x 11 = 77 lands on 25. 7 x 19 = 133 lands on 3, not 1. (Stage: 'your 7 × 11 = 77 → 25' on the ring and in the ×7 summary row.)
claims.source: 77 = 2 x 26 + 25; 133 = 5 x 26 + 3 (builder's node script, 2026-10-14). Shown in the reveal only to learners who picked 11 or 19. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: node: 77 % 26 = 25, 133 % 26 = 3 (133 = 5 x 26 + 3). Reveal branches on prediction 0 and 2 only. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v2, wave E r6 revision by demo-builder): stage now has a 26-hour ring and a ×13 chip; reveal reworded and shortened. | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. node: 77 % 26 = 25, 133 % 26 = 3. Reveal branches on prediction 0 (11) and 2 (19) only. Ring label 'your 7 x 11 = 77 -> 25' shows when on x7 and x has been read off; the x13 view's summary row shows the same text once read.

claims.text: If 1 = a x 26 + b x 7, then b undoes multiplying by 7. An undo exists exactly when the gcd is 1.
claims.source: Derivation: reducing mod 26 gives b x 7 = 1 (mod 26). Conversely, if 7b = 1 (mod 26) then 7b - 1 = k x 26, so any common divisor of 7 and 26 divides 1. Existence when the gcd is 1 is Bezout's identity, produced by extended Euclid: CLRS 4e chapter 31 (section 31.2, EXTENDED-EUCLID; section 31.4, Corollary on the inverse mod n existing iff gcd(a, n) = 1). · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: Verdict rests on the derivation (both directions re-done; existence when gcd = 1 is exactly what extended Euclid constructs, as on the stage). CLRS 4e 31.2/31.4 cited from memory, not opened. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v2, wave E r6 revision by demo-builder): stage now has a 26-hour ring and a ×13 chip; reveal reworded and shortened. | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Rests on the derivation, not on CLRS (not opened): b x 7 = 1 (mod 26) from reducing 1 = a x 26 + b x 7; conversely 7b - 1 = k x 26 means any common divisor of 7 and 26 divides 1; extended Euclid constructs a, b when gcd = 1. Reveal: 'An undo exists exactly when the gcd is 1'.

claims.text: 12 of the 25 non-zero hours on a 26-hour clock have an undo.
claims.source: Demo.tsx INVERTIBLE counts a in 1..25 with gcd(a, 26) = 1: 12 (the odd numbers other than 13). Builder's node script (2026-10-14): 13x mod 26 is only ever 0 or 13, never 1. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: node: a in 1..25 with gcd(a,26)=1 -> 12 (odd numbers except 13); 13x mod 26 takes only 0 and 13. Matches Demo INVERTIBLE. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v2, wave E r6 revision by demo-builder): stage now has a 26-hour ring and a ×13 chip; reveal reworded and shortened. | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. node: a in 1..25 with gcd(a, 26) = 1 -> 12 (odd numbers except 13) = Demo INVERTIBLE; reveal '12 of the 25 non-zero hours'.

claims.text: This is the step RSA uses to make a private key.
claims.source: RSA's private exponent d is the multiplicative inverse of the public exponent e modulo phi(n), computed with extended Euclid: Rivest, Shamir and Adleman, 'A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-Key Cryptosystems', CACM 21(2), 1978; CLRS 4e chapter 31 (section 31.7, the RSA public-key cryptosystem). · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: Rivest-Shamir-Adleman paper and CLRS not opened (hosts blocked). Web-search results (CACM 21(2):120-126, 1978; lecture notes e.g. Rosulek ch. 13, Grenet RSA slides) state d = e^-1 mod phi(n), computed by extended Euclid. Verified on those secondary sources; the learner sentence is general and does not quote the paper. | WITHDRAWN 2026-10-14 (v2) by demo-builder: RSA context sentence cut to keep the reveal under budget after the ×13 sentence was added.

claims.text: On a 26-hour clock, 7x for x = 0 to 25 lands on all 26 hours; 13x lands on only 0 and 13, so no x makes 13x land on 1. (Stage ring captions: '×7: x = 0…25 lands on all 26 hours' / '×13: x = 0…25 lands on only 0 and 13'.)
claims.source: 13x mod 26 is 0 for even x and 13 for odd x; gcd(7, 26) = 1 so x -> 7x mod 26 is a bijection. Demo.tsx hits(). | Added 2026-10-14 (v2) by demo-builder. | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own copy of hits(): x7 over x = 0..25 gives 26 distinct hours; x13 gives {0, 13}. Captions 'lands on all 26 hours' / 'lands on only 0 and 13' match.

claims.text: With 13, Euclid stops at 13, not 1: 26 = 2 x 13 + 0, so 1 cannot be written as a mix of 26 and 13 and x13 has no undo. (Stage: 'gcd = 13, not 1: no way to write 1. ×13 has no undo.')
claims.source: Euclid(26, 13): one row, remainder 0, gcd 13. Any a x 26 + b x 13 is a multiple of 13, so never 1 (Demo.tsx euclid(N, B)). | Added 2026-10-14 (v2) by demo-builder. | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own euclid(26, 13): r = [26, 13, 0], q = [2]: one row '26 = 2 x 13 + 0', gcd 13. Any a x 26 + b x 13 is a multiple of 13, so never 1. Stage note 'gcd = 13, not 1: no way to write 1. x13 has no undo.' and readout 'Undo x13: none' after the no-undo milestone.

recall.question: On a 10-hour clock, can you undo multiplying by 4?
options: No: 4 and 10 share the factor 2, so 4x never lands on 1
Yes: divide by 4, as on a number line
Yes: run Euclid on 10 and 4 backwards to find x
recall.why: An undo exists exactly when the gcd is 1. Here gcd(4, 10) = 2: 4x is always even, and so is 4x minus any multiple of 10, so it can never be 1.
